gloss: spell · incantation · mantra — also to curse
form: Mojidata IDS: 吅 (two mouths) + 几
formNote: The Shuowen has no entry for 咒; it is a later graph (also written 呪) commonly related to 祝, “to invoke”. The two mouths of 吅 make it a graph of speaking twice over. Its everyday sense is “to curse”.
summary: A spoken formula with power: a spell, a curse, and in Buddhist texts the mantra and the dhāraṇī. Some are translated; the most important are carried by sound alone, because what they are is how they sound.
placement: On the far left of the band, beside 如 and 真: the spoken formula at the edge of speech. (Placement is a design choice, not a claim.)

oc.note: † Baracus’s guess by way of 祝 (*[t]uk); uncertain. Check B–S 2014 for 呪 / 咒.

satellites.title: 陀羅尼: What Holds
satellites.evidence: Dhāraṇī, from dhṛ, “to hold”, is a formula that holds a teaching in memory. Chinese both transcribes it by sound, 陀羅尼, and translates it, 總持, “holding all”, and often simply calls it 咒.

satellites.title: Gone, Gone Beyond
satellites.evidence: The Heart Sutra ends with its mantra, given by sound, not meaning: 揭諦揭諦，波羅揭諦，波羅僧揭諦，菩提薩婆訶 (gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā). A mantra crosses languages as sound; to translate it would change what it is.

satellites.title: Invocation and Curse
satellites.evidence: The Shuowen lists 祝, 祭主贊詞者, “the one who speaks the praises at a sacrifice”. 咒 is commonly treated as a later form of the same word: the invoker’s speech, which can bless or curse.
satellites.caveat: The relation of 咒 to 祝 is the common view, drafted by Baracus from general knowledge; it needs a palaeographic source.
gaps: Cite a source for 咒 / 呪 as a later form of 祝.
